title: The Script That Used to Work
body: You've delivered the same termination speech 200 times. 'This isn't a reflection of your performance.' You believe it less each time. Today the departing engineer cried and you felt nothing. Then you felt something about feeling nothing. You drove home in silence and sat in the driveway for twenty minutes.

choices.title: Rewrite the script to feel human again
choices.body: Spend the weekend rewriting the termination script with actual honesty.

choices.title: Book a therapy session, finally
choices.body: The company EAP covers six sessions. You've earned all six.

choices.title: Pour wine, open LinkedIn, doom scroll
choices.body: Numb it with Pinot Grigio and other people's career announcements.

title: The Algorithm Reads Resumes Now
body: The new ATS uses AI to screen resumes. It rejected a candidate you hand-picked because their formatting was 'non-standard.' The candidate had fifteen years of experience. The AI preferred a fresh grad who used the right template. You stare at the rejection dashboard like it owes you an apology.

choices.title: Override the AI and push your candidate
choices.body: Manually advance the candidate. The machine doesn't know people.

choices.title: Train the AI with better rubrics
choices.body: Spend a week teaching the algorithm what actually matters in a hire.

choices.title: Let it go, the hiring manager won't notice
choices.body: The hiring manager wanted 'top of funnel speed.' This is what speed looks like.

title: DEI Budget Cut to Zero
body: The CFO eliminated the DEI budget in a line item labeled 'non-essential programs.' Your ERG leads are furious. The CEO's statement says 'we remain deeply committed to inclusion' in the same email that killed the inclusion budget. You have to deliver the news at the next ERG meeting. The room will be full of people who trusted you.

choices.title: Fight for partial funding in the next cycle
choices.body: Build a business case with retention data and present it to the CFO directly.

choices.title: Deliver the news with honesty, skip the spin
choices.body: Tell the ERG leads the truth. No corporate euphemisms. They deserve that.

choices.title: Wordsmith the announcement until it means nothing
choices.body: Write a memo so polished it reflects no light and contains no information.

title: Culture Fit as a Blunt Instrument
body: A hiring manager rejected a stellar candidate for 'not being a culture fit.' The candidate was qualified, experienced, and different from everyone on the team. The manager can't articulate what 'culture fit' means but is very sure this person doesn't have it. You've seen this movie before. The ending is always the same.

choices.title: Push back and document the pattern
choices.body: Flag the pattern formally. Risk becoming the person nobody wants in hiring meetings.

choices.title: Coach the manager on structured interviews
choices.body: Redirect the energy into process improvement. Scorecards over vibes.

choices.title: Let it slide, pick your battles
choices.body: You can't fight every hiring manager. You'd never stop fighting.

title: The PIP Assembly Line
body: Legal wants you to put three more people on performance improvement plans this quarter. Everyone knows PIPs are termination paperwork with extra steps. You write the improvement goals knowing they're designed to be unfailable — and also unpassable. The word 'measurable' appears eleven times. None of the measurements matter.

choices.title: Write real goals that could actually help
choices.body: Make the PIPs genuine. Give people a real chance. Legal will hate it.

choices.title: Process the paperwork and move on
choices.body: The system wants documentation. You produce documentation. That's the job.

choices.title: Warn the employees off the record
choices.body: Quietly tell them to start looking. It's not in your job description. It should be.

title: The Holiday Party Nobody Wants You At
body: The holiday party. Everyone goes silent when you approach a group. Someone literally changes the subject. You know everyone's salary, their performance ratings, who's on a PIP, and who's about to be let go. You are the human embodiment of privileged information standing by the cheese platter. The cheese is fine. The loneliness is not.

choices.title: Leave early, watch Netflix in pajamas
choices.body: Two glasses of wine and a graceful exit. You've mastered this.

choices.title: Force yourself to stay and make small talk
choices.body: Be a human for one night. Ask someone about their weekend. Mean it.

choices.title: Befriend the other lonely executive at the bar
choices.body: The CFO is also standing alone. You bond over being workplace villains.

title: Someone Leaked the Layoff List
body: The layoff list leaked on Blind. Your name isn't on it — you wrote it. The comments are brutal. 'HR are just professional liars with benefits.' 'They smile while they fire you.' Someone posted a screenshot of your team's Glassdoor response to a negative review. The response is corporate poetry. You wrote that too.

choices.title: Investigate the leak professionally
choices.body: Follow the process. Contain the damage. Pretend it doesn't sting.

choices.title: Read every comment until 2am
choices.body: You shouldn't. You will. Every word lands like a small accurate knife.

choices.title: Talk to a trusted colleague about the toll
choices.body: Someone outside the blast radius. Someone who might still see you as a person.

title: Chatbot Wants Your Onboarding Job
body: The VP of Engineering wants to pilot an AI chatbot for new hire onboarding. 'It can answer questions 24/7,' he says, as if the value of onboarding was answering questions about the parking policy at midnight. You built the onboarding program from scratch. It has a 92% satisfaction score. The chatbot demo scored 94%.

choices.title: Propose a hybrid: chatbot for logistics, you for humans
choices.body: Let the bot handle parking. You handle the part where someone feels welcome.

choices.title: Let the pilot run and document every failure
choices.body: Give it enough rope. Keep detailed notes. Patience is a strategy.

choices.title: Block the pilot with compliance concerns
choices.body: Data privacy, SOC 2, new hire PII — there are real concerns. And convenient ones.

title: The Emotional Labor Has No Line Item
body: You spent three hours consoling a manager who had to deliver bad news to their team. Before that, you mediated a conflict between two directors. Before that, you talked someone out of quitting. None of this is in your job description. Your job description says 'administer benefits' and 'ensure compliance.' Your actual job is being everyone's therapist without a license.

choices.title: Set boundaries and redirect to EAP
choices.body: You are not a therapist. Start acting like it. Refer them to professionals.

choices.title: Keep absorbing it, it's what you're good at
choices.body: The company runs on your emotional bandwidth. You just don't get paid for it.

choices.title: Document the hours and pitch a wellness role
choices.body: If emotional labor is this much of the job, make it an actual job.

title: The Exit Interview That Got Too Real
body: A departing senior engineer looks you in the eye during their exit interview and says, 'You know this place is broken, right? You know, and you stay anyway.' The recording light is on. You should redirect to the structured questions. Instead you sit there for a moment too long. The silence says everything the form won't capture.

choices.title: Redirect to the form and stay professional
choices.body: Click the next question. Maintain the boundary. That's the job.

choices.title: Turn off the recorder and have a real conversation
choices.body: Off the record. Human to human. Just this once.

choices.title: Include the raw feedback in the report to leadership
choices.body: Let the truth reach the people who need to hear it. Brace for impact.

title: The Pay Transparency Bomb
body: New state law requires salary ranges on job postings. You know exactly how many current employees are below the posted minimum for their own role. Seventeen people. Some by a lot. The recruiter asks if you want to 'adjust the ranges.' You know what that means. It means lying with numbers instead of words.

choices.title: Flag the pay gaps to leadership with a fix plan
choices.body: Equity adjustment proposals. Data-backed. Uncomfortable. Necessary.

choices.title: Post honest ranges and let the chips fall
choices.body: The law is the law. Let the internal questions come.

choices.title: Fudge the ranges to avoid internal chaos
choices.body: Technically compliant. Morally exhausting. Welcome to HR.

title: Nobody Comes to Your Trainings
body: You built a manager training on giving effective feedback. Eight people registered. Two showed up. One was on their phone. The other asked if this would 'count toward their OKRs.' You spent forty hours on the curriculum. The slide deck is genuinely good. Nobody will ever know.

choices.title: Make it mandatory and tie it to promotion criteria
choices.body: If they won't come voluntarily, make it required. This is how policy works.

choices.title: Record it as async content and move on
choices.body: On-demand video. Let the algorithm surface it. Lower expectations.

choices.title: Cancel the program and let managers fail
choices.body: You can lead a horse to water. The horse is on Slack and doesn't drink water.

title: Glassdoor Reputation Management
body: The CEO wants you to 'fix' the Glassdoor rating. It's 2.8 stars. The top review says 'HR is complicit.' You've been asked to encourage happy employees to leave positive reviews. This is technically not against the rules. It is spiritually bankrupt. You open a draft response that begins 'Thank you for your candid feedback.'

choices.title: Write authentic responses and push for real change
choices.body: Respond honestly. Advocate internally. Play the long game.

choices.title: Campaign for positive reviews from engaged employees
choices.body: Ask happy people to be loud. It's not manipulation. It's amplification. Right?

choices.title: Tell the CEO the rating reflects reality
choices.body: The rating is accurate. Say so. Watch the temperature in the room drop.

title: The AI Mood Ring
body: Someone installed an AI sentiment analysis tool on company Slack. It generates a daily 'morale score.' Today the score is 34 out of 100. The tool flagged twelve employees as 'flight risks' based on their message patterns. One of them used the word 'frustrated' in a message about a JavaScript framework. The dashboard doesn't know the difference between code frustration and existential dread.

choices.title: Kill the tool, it's surveillance dressed as wellness
choices.body: Pull the plug. Explain to leadership why monitoring Slack morale is dystopian.

choices.title: Refine the tool with better training data
choices.body: The concept isn't wrong, the execution is. Make it less stupid.

choices.title: Use it but never tell employees it exists
choices.body: The data is useful. The optics are not. Compartmentalize.

title: Layoff Round Two
body: Six months after the last round, the CFO needs another 15% cut. The people left are already doing the work of two. Morale is a memory. You have to build the list again. The spreadsheet columns are the same: name, title, salary, severance cost. There's no column for 'has a newborn' or 'just bought a house.' You add those columns anyway. Nobody asks why.

choices.title: Fight for better severance packages
choices.body: If they're cutting, at least make the landing softer. Advocate for the humans.

choices.title: Execute efficiently and contain the blast radius
choices.body: Fast and clean. The longer it drags, the worse it gets for everyone.

choices.title: Start your own exit plan quietly
choices.body: If they're cutting this deep, your department is next. Update the resume.

title: The Benefits Broker Goes AI
body: Your benefits broker replaced their account team with an AI assistant. Benefits questions now go to a chatbot named 'Benny.' An employee with a cancer diagnosis just spent forty minutes arguing with Benny about prior authorization. They came to your desk in tears. Benny's satisfaction score is 4.2 stars. This employee would rate it differently.

choices.title: Escalate to the broker and demand human support
choices.body: Call the broker. Demand a human. Threaten to switch providers.

choices.title: Help the employee directly, bypass the system
choices.body: Sit with them. Make the calls yourself. This is the job that matters.

choices.title: Document the failure and build a case for switching
choices.body: One story is an anecdote. A spreadsheet of failures is a procurement decision.

title: The Return to Office Mandate
body: Leadership wants everyone back five days a week. You have to enforce it. The policy was written by people with corner offices and fifteen-minute commutes. A single mom on the team moved two hours away during remote work. A disabled employee's accommodation request is 'under review.' You are the face of a decision you didn't make and don't agree with.

choices.title: Enforce it fairly and process exceptions by the book
choices.body: Apply the policy consistently. Push accommodation requests through fast.

choices.title: Quietly approve every exception you can justify
choices.body: Use every loophole in the policy to protect the people who need it.

choices.title: Present leadership with attrition projections
choices.body: Show them the math. Twelve people will quit. Replacing them costs more than flexibility.

title: The AI Scheduler From Hell
body: The AI interview scheduling tool booked a candidate for 6am on a Sunday. The candidate is in a different timezone. The tool doesn't understand timezones the way humans do, which is to say it doesn't understand timezones at all. The candidate showed up anyway. You feel worse about that than the error.

choices.title: Fix the tool settings and send a personal apology
choices.body: Apologize like a human. Fix the machine. Hope the candidate forgives both.

choices.title: Switch back to manual scheduling for now
choices.body: Sometimes the old way is the right way. Calendly still works.

choices.title: Report it as a bug and keep using the tool
choices.body: One error doesn't kill a system. Log it, flag it, move on.

title: The Survivors' Meeting
body: After the layoffs, you hold a 'moving forward' meeting for the remaining team. Someone asks 'are we safe?' and you say 'we're focused on the future' which is HR for 'I genuinely don't know.' The room can hear what you're not saying. They've learned to read you like a legal document — it's what's missing that matters.

choices.title: Be as transparent as you're allowed to be
choices.body: Say what you can. Acknowledge the uncertainty. It's not much but it's honest.

choices.title: Stick to the approved talking points
choices.body: Legal reviewed this script. Your job is to read it. Nothing more.

choices.title: Open the floor and let people vent
choices.body: Forget the agenda. Let them be angry. Absorb it. That's what you're here for.

title: AI Wrote the Compliance Training
body: You outsourced the annual compliance training to an AI content platform. It generated forty slides on harassment prevention in six minutes. The content is technically accurate and completely soulless. Slide 14 uses the phrase 'inappropriate physical interface.' Your old version took three weeks and people still clicked through without reading. Maybe soulless is fine.

choices.title: Use the AI version and save three weeks
choices.body: Nobody reads compliance training anyway. Efficient soullessness wins.

choices.title: Rewrite the worst slides with human examples
choices.body: Hybrid approach. Let the AI draft, but make the important parts real.

choices.title: Scrap it and build interactive workshops instead
choices.body: Slides don't change behavior. Conversations do. Go back to basics.

title: Empathy on Empty
body: Three terminations before lunch. A harassment complaint after. A crying manager at 4pm. You smiled through all of it. Your face hurts from performing compassion. In the parking lot you realize you can't remember any of their names. Not because you don't care. Because you cared too many times today and something in you just... buffered.

choices.title: Take a personal day tomorrow, no guilt
choices.body: One day off. No emails. The company will survive without your feelings.

choices.title: Call a friend who doesn't work in HR
choices.body: Someone who doesn't know what a PIP is. Someone who still thinks HR plans parties.

choices.title: Push through, you've had worse weeks
choices.body: This is the job. You chose it. Pour another coffee and keep going.

title: The LinkedIn Hot Take Backfires
body: You posted a thoughtful piece about the emotional toll of layoffs. It went semi-viral. Mostly supportive comments. Then a laid-off employee from your company commented: 'Easy to talk about empathy when you're the one holding the axe.' Three hundred likes on that reply. Your DMs are a war zone.

choices.title: Respond thoughtfully and own the contradiction
choices.body: Acknowledge the tension publicly. You are both the system and a person in it.

choices.title: Delete the post and go dark for a week
choices.body: Some conversations aren't worth having in public. Retreat.

choices.title: DM the commenter privately and listen
choices.body: Take it offline. Hear them out. Maybe they're right.

title: The AI Reference Checker
body: A vendor pitches an AI that conducts reference checks via text message. No phone calls, no human interaction. The AI asks structured questions and flags inconsistencies. A reference for a candidate replied 'lol what is this' and the AI logged it as 'respondent expressed confusion, possible concern about candidate.' You're watching the future of trust get automated.

choices.title: Reject the tool and keep doing phone references
choices.body: References are about tone, pauses, what people don't say. AI can't hear silence.

choices.title: Pilot it for high-volume roles only
choices.body: Use it where speed matters. Keep humans for the roles where nuance matters.

choices.title: Use it but review every AI-flagged result yourself
choices.body: Let the machine filter. You make the calls. Literally.

title: The Curse of Knowing Everyone's Salary
body: You're at happy hour with colleagues. Someone complains about being underpaid. You know they're the highest-paid person at their level. The person next to them, who laughs and says 'same,' actually is underpaid — by $40,000. You sip your drink and say nothing. This is what it's like to carry information you can never use.

choices.title: Encourage them to research market rates
choices.body: You can't tell them what you know. You can point them where to look.

choices.title: Change the subject to anything else
choices.body: How about those local sports teams. Literally anything but compensation.

choices.title: Quietly advocate for the underpaid one in the next review cycle
choices.body: You can't say it out loud but you can move the numbers where it matters.

title: Wellness Program as Theater
body: The company launched a wellness initiative. Yoga on Tuesdays. A meditation app nobody uses. A Slack channel called #self-care that's mostly memes. Meanwhile, people are working 55-hour weeks and the on-call rotation is destroying the engineering team's sleep. You organized the yoga. You know it's a band-aid on a bullet wound.

choices.title: Push for systemic changes instead of perks
choices.body: Kill the yoga. Fix the on-call rotation. Address the actual problem.

choices.title: Keep the wellness perks, they help some people
choices.body: Not everything has to be systemic. Some people actually like the yoga.

choices.title: Write a Medium post about corporate wellness theater
choices.body: Say the quiet part loud. Burn a bridge or two. Maybe start a conversation.

title: The Euphemism Industrial Complex
body: 'Rightsizing.' 'Organizational realignment.' 'Workforce optimization.' 'Role elimination.' You've written all of these in official communications. Each one means the same thing: someone is losing their job. You've become fluent in a language designed to make pain invisible. Sometimes you catch yourself using it at home. 'I'm going to optimize the dishwasher situation.'

choices.title: Start using plain language in official comms
choices.body: Say 'layoffs' when you mean layoffs. See how long it lasts.

choices.title: Draft a lexicon of what corporate phrases really mean
choices.body: A private document. For your sanity. To remember what words are supposed to mean.

choices.title: Lean into it, the euphemisms protect everyone
choices.body: Maybe the soft language helps people process. Maybe you need to believe that.

title: Practicing the Firing Conversation
body: You're coaching a first-time manager on how to terminate someone. You role-play the conversation. You play the employee. You say 'But I have a family' with such conviction that the manager tears up. You've done this exercise fifty times. You know exactly which words break people. That knowledge lives in you like scar tissue.

choices.title: Coach them to be direct and humane
choices.body: Teach them: clear, fast, kind. Don't read a script. Be a person.

choices.title: Give them the script and let them figure it out
choices.body: They'll learn the way you learned. By doing it badly the first time.

choices.title: Offer to sit in on the actual conversation
choices.body: Be in the room. They shouldn't have to do this alone their first time.

title: The HR Conference Circuit
body: You're at an HR tech conference. Every booth has the word 'AI' in it. Every demo promises to 'revolutionize the employee experience.' A vendor asks if you want to see their AI-powered exit interview tool. You've spent fifteen years perfecting exit interviews. The demo takes four minutes. It's not terrible. That's the part that stings.

choices.title: Network hard and collect every business card
choices.body: Ignore the booths. Talk to the people. Build your external network.

choices.title: Test every AI tool and take detailed notes
choices.body: Know your enemy. Or your replacement. Same thing.

choices.title: Skip the expo, hit the bar with other HR leaders
choices.body: The real conference happens after hours. Everyone's more honest with a drink.

title: The Anonymous Feedback Is Not Anonymous
body: The anonymous feedback tool has a bug. You can see who wrote what. You weren't supposed to look. You looked. An employee wrote: 'HR exists to protect the company, not us. Everyone knows this.' Another wrote: 'She seems nice but she's basically a corporate lawyer with a smile.' You close the tab. You can't un-know this.

choices.title: Report the bug and never mention what you saw
choices.body: Fix the system. Bury the knowledge. Carry it like everything else.

choices.title: Use the feedback to quietly improve your approach
choices.body: They're not wrong. Let the truth make you better, even if they never know.

choices.title: Disclose the bug to employees and reset trust
choices.body: Tell everyone. Reset the survey. Eat the embarrassment. Rebuild.

title: People Ops Becomes People Analytics
body: Your title changed from 'HR Manager' to 'People Analytics Lead.' Your job description now includes 'data-driven workforce insights' and 'predictive attrition modeling.' You don't know Python. You don't know SQL. You know people. The new title suggests that's no longer enough.

choices.title: Learn SQL and lean into the analytics pivot
choices.body: If the job is changing, change with it. Stack Overflow at midnight.

choices.title: Push back on the rebrand and defend the human side
choices.body: Analytics without empathy is just surveillance with charts.

choices.title: Hire a data person and become their translator
choices.body: Bridge the gap. You speak human. They speak SQL. Together you're useful.

title: The Manager Who Won't Follow the Script
body: A director fired someone without consulting HR. No documentation. No final warning. No witness. The employee is lawyering up. You're doing damage control for a mess you didn't make. The director says 'I don't need HR to tell me how to run my team.' Legal says you need a time machine.

choices.title: Document everything and contain the legal exposure
choices.body: Damage control mode. Paper trail. Incident report. CYA.

choices.title: Escalate to the CEO with the legal risk assessment
choices.body: This director just created a lawsuit. Leadership needs to know. Today.

choices.title: Reach out to the fired employee yourself
choices.body: Offer to help them navigate the situation. It's not standard. It's right.

title: Firing Your First Work Friend
body: The list came down and Sarah's name is on it. Sarah who brought you coffee when you had a migraine. Sarah who texted you on your birthday. Sarah who is about to sit across from you while you read a script about 'organizational changes.' You practiced the speech in the mirror this morning. Your reflection looked like a stranger.

choices.title: Deliver the news with as much humanity as possible
choices.body: Look her in the eye. Don't rush. Let her feel what she needs to feel.

choices.title: Ask someone else to handle this one
choices.body: You can't be objective. Recuse yourself. It's not weakness. It's honesty.

choices.title: Do it yourself and call her after with real words
choices.body: Be the professional in the room. Be the friend afterward.

title: The Demo That Does Your Job
body: A sales rep demos an HR automation platform. It handles onboarding, offboarding, benefits enrollment, compliance tracking, and employee queries. 'This replaces about 2.5 FTEs,' he says cheerfully. You are 1.0 FTE. You smile and take notes. The notes say 'this is how I die, professionally.'

choices.title: Evaluate it honestly and recommend what works
choices.body: If parts of your job should be automated, say so. Credibility matters more than territory.

choices.title: Find every flaw and present a cautious assessment
choices.body: The demo was polished. Reality won't be. Highlight the gaps.

choices.title: Start positioning yourself for the role that manages the platform
choices.body: If the machine is coming, become the person who runs the machine.

title: The Engagement Survey Ritual
body: Annual engagement survey results are in. Engagement is down 12 points. The lowest-scoring question: 'I trust leadership to make decisions in my best interest.' You wrote that question. You also don't trust leadership to make decisions in your best interest. You prepare a presentation that says 'opportunity areas' instead of 'everything is on fire.'

choices.title: Present the data raw and let leadership react
choices.body: No spin. No softening. Here are the numbers. Here is what they mean.

choices.title: Package it with recommendations they might actually do
choices.body: Make it actionable. Small wins. Baby steps toward not being terrible.

choices.title: Bury the worst numbers in an appendix nobody reads
choices.body: The truth is in the deck. Just not on slide one. Technically transparent.

title: The HR Influencer Pipeline
body: Every HR person on LinkedIn seems to be building a personal brand. 'Thought leader.' 'People strategist.' 'Culture architect.' They post daily about 'the future of work' with ring lights and branded slides. You have fifteen years of experience and zero followers. The algorithm doesn't care about experience. It cares about consistency and confidence. You have neither at 9pm on a Tuesday.

choices.title: Start posting weekly about what HR really looks like
choices.body: No ring light. No jargon. Just the truth about being the person in the middle.

choices.title: Ignore LinkedIn and focus on being good at the actual job
choices.body: Personal brands are for people who need an audience. You need sleep.

choices.title: Reach out to an HR influencer for mentorship
choices.body: Maybe they know something you don't. Or maybe they just post better. Either way, ask.

title: The AI Interviewer Outperforms You
body: The company piloted AI-conducted first-round interviews. Structured questions, consistent scoring, no unconscious bias — at least none they can measure. Candidates rated the AI interviewer higher than human interviewers. One candidate said 'it felt less judgmental.' You've spent a decade training interviewers. The machine just skipped the decade.

choices.title: Become the AI interview designer
choices.body: If the machine is interviewing, someone still designs the questions. Be that person.

choices.title: Argue for keeping humans in the loop
choices.body: Interviews are about chemistry, not checklists. Push to keep humans in round one.

choices.title: Study the AI's scoring rubric and learn from it
choices.body: The machine is consistent in ways you never were. That's humbling and useful.

title: Performance Reviews by Algorithm
body: Performance reviews are now 'AI-assisted.' The system aggregates Slack activity, commit history, meeting attendance, and 360 feedback into a single score. A top performer got a 62 because she works asynchronously and doesn't use Slack much. A mediocre employee got a 91 because he's in every meeting and messages constantly. The algorithm rewards visibility, not value.

choices.title: Override the scores and calibrate manually
choices.body: Add human judgment back. Fight the dashboard with a spreadsheet.

choices.title: Present the flaws to leadership with examples
choices.body: Show them what the algorithm actually measures. It's not performance.

choices.title: Let the scores stand, that's what they asked for
choices.body: They wanted data-driven reviews. This is what data-driven looks like.

title: The Chatbot Ate Your Inbox
body: An HR chatbot now handles 80% of employee inquiries. PTO balance, benefits questions, policy lookups — all automated. Your inbox went from 200 emails a day to 40. You should feel relieved. Instead you feel like a lighthouse keeper watching ships install GPS. The light still works. Nobody needs it.

choices.title: Redirect your time to strategic work
choices.body: Use the freed-up hours to focus on retention strategy and culture work.

choices.title: Monitor the chatbot for errors obsessively
choices.body: Become the chatbot's quality assurance team. Make yourself necessary.

choices.title: Volunteer for a cross-functional project
choices.body: If HR needs less of you, find somewhere that needs more of you.

title: Am I the System or a Person
body: In a leadership meeting, the CEO refers to HR as 'a function, not a team.' You're sitting right there. Later, in a 1:1, your direct report asks 'do you ever feel like we're just... infrastructure?' You don't answer immediately. The pause lasts long enough for both of you to hear the HVAC system, which is also infrastructure, and working perfectly fine, and no one thanks it either.

choices.title: Redefine the HR team's value proposition
choices.body: If they see you as infrastructure, show them what breaks when the infrastructure stops.

choices.title: Start journaling about what you actually want
choices.body: Not what the job needs. What you need. When did you stop asking?

choices.title: Accept the infrastructure role and optimize it
choices.body: Plumbing keeps people alive. There's dignity in that. Maybe.

title: They Want the Chatbot to Fire People
body: The VP of Operations asks if the termination chatbot can 'handle the initial notification.' Not the paperwork — the actual conversation. 'It would reduce emotional variance,' he says, as if human emotion during job loss is a bug to be patched. You stare at him for three seconds too long. He adds, 'Just exploring options.'

choices.title: Shut it down immediately and hard
choices.body: No. Absolutely not. Some things require a human face. This is the line.

choices.title: Write a formal policy against AI-conducted terminations
choices.body: Put it in writing before someone else puts it in production.

choices.title: Ask for a pilot on voluntary separations only
choices.body: Test the boundary carefully. People leaving by choice is different. Maybe.

title: The Dashboard That Knows Too Much
body: Your new people analytics dashboard predicts employee departures with 87% accuracy. It flagged your best recruiter as a flight risk. The recruiter hasn't told anyone she's interviewing. You know because the algorithm noticed her LinkedIn activity spike, her meeting pattern change, and her Slack response time increase. You feel like a corporate spy with a wellness mandate.

choices.title: Use the data to proactively improve her experience
choices.body: Don't confront her. Fix the things making her want to leave.

choices.title: Ignore the prediction and respect her privacy
choices.body: People are allowed to explore options. Knowing doesn't mean acting.

choices.title: Raise ethical concerns about predictive surveillance
choices.body: Flag this to leadership. This tool is a liability dressed as insight.

title: AI Writes Better Job Descriptions Than You
body: You spent four hours crafting an inclusive, compelling job description. Then you ran it through an AI rewriter 'just to see.' The AI version got 3x more applications in A/B testing. It used words you would never choose. It felt generic. It worked better. Your craft lost to a prompt.

choices.title: Adopt the AI approach and focus on what converts
choices.body: Results matter more than pride. Let the data win.

choices.title: Blend both approaches and create your own templates
choices.body: Use the AI's structure with your voice. Own the middle ground.

choices.title: Question whether more applications means better candidates
choices.body: Volume isn't quality. Maybe your version attracted the right people.

title: The Executive Coaching Side Hustle
body: A former colleague now charges $400/hour as an executive coach. She left HR two years ago and posts sunset photos with captions about 'aligned leadership.' Her calendar is full. Your calendar is full of termination meetings. Same skill set. Different packaging. You could do what she does. The question is whether you should.

choices.title: Start coaching on the side, test the waters
choices.body: Evenings and weekends. Build the portfolio. See if the market bites.

choices.title: Reach out to her for advice on making the jump
choices.body: She did it. Ask how. Swallow the envy. Learn the playbook.

choices.title: Stay in HR and build internal coaching programs
choices.body: The skills translate. Use them where you are. Create value from the inside.

title: The AI Mediator
body: A startup pitches an AI conflict resolution tool. Two employees describe their issue to the chatbot, it identifies the underlying interests, and proposes a resolution. In the demo it resolved a six-month territorial dispute in twelve minutes. Your last mediation of a similar dispute took three weeks and ended with one person transferring departments. The AI doesn't get tired. It doesn't take sides. It also doesn't know that Janet's husband just left her and that's why she's been difficult.

choices.title: Pilot it for low-stakes conflicts
choices.body: Scheduling disputes and desk assignments. Keep the human stuff for humans.

choices.title: Reject it and defend the value of human mediation
choices.body: Conflict isn't a logic problem. It's an emotional one. Machines can't hold space.

choices.title: Buy it and use it to prep for your own mediations
choices.body: Let the AI do the analysis. You do the empathy. Best of both worlds.

title: Lunch Alone Again
body: You eat lunch at your desk for the third week straight. Not because you're busy — because nobody invites you. The marketing team has a lunch group. Engineering has their thing. You are cordially excluded from all of it. Someone once told you 'it's not personal, it's just... you know too much.' You know. That's the problem.

choices.title: Join a lunch group outside the company
choices.body: Find humans who don't flinch when you say where you work. They exist.

choices.title: Invite a new employee who doesn't know the politics yet
choices.body: Someone who still sees you as a person, not a department. Enjoy it while it lasts.

choices.title: Lean into the solitude, use lunch to plan your exit
choices.body: Alone time is strategy time. Start building something outside these walls.

title: Restructuring Your Own Department
body: The irony. You've restructured every department in the company. Now leadership wants you to restructure HR. Cut two headcount from your team of five. You have to choose who stays. These are your people. The ones who've had your back through every layoff, every lawsuit, every 2am Slack crisis. The spreadsheet needs two names. Your hands don't want to type them.

choices.title: Propose automating tasks instead of cutting people
choices.body: Show how AI tools can absorb the workload. Save the humans. Use the machines.

choices.title: Make the cuts and carry the weight
choices.body: You've asked others to do this. Now it's your turn. Don't flinch.

choices.title: Volunteer yourself for the cut instead
choices.body: Take the severance. Spare your team. Maybe this is the exit you've been waiting for.

title: The AI Diversity Optimizer
body: A tool promises to 'optimize hiring pipelines for diversity outcomes.' It adjusts which candidates are surfaced based on demographic targets. It's technically not quotas — it's 'algorithmic pipeline balancing.' Legal says it's a gray area. The EEOC would have opinions. The DEI team loves it. You're caught between doing the right thing and doing the thing that might be illegal.

choices.title: Block it until legal gives an explicit green light
choices.body: Good intentions don't survive lawsuits. Get it in writing first.

choices.title: Implement it quietly and track outcomes
choices.body: If it works, nobody will question it. If it doesn't, you'll shut it down.

choices.title: Advocate for structural changes instead of algorithmic fixes
choices.body: Diversity isn't a pipeline problem. It's a culture problem. Fix the culture.

title: You're Burned Out From Running the Burnout Survey
body: The burnout survey results show 67% of employees are experiencing burnout. You're one of them. You can't put yourself on the action plan. You present the findings with a steady voice and tired eyes. Someone asks 'what is HR doing about this?' The answer is: HR is burning out trying to measure how burned out everyone else is.

choices.title: Be honest about your own burnout in the meeting
choices.body: Model vulnerability. Say 'me too.' See what happens when the messenger is also the message.

choices.title: Delegate the action plan and take a week off
choices.body: You can't pour from an empty cup. The metaphor is tired because you're tired.

choices.title: Push through and deliver the plan on time
choices.body: The irony is noted. The deadline doesn't care about irony.

title: The Algorithm Sets Salaries Now
body: A new AI compensation benchmarking tool recommends pay ranges based on market data, internal equity, and performance scores. It recommended cutting three people's salaries. It recommended a 40% raise for the intern. The algorithm doesn't know the intern is the CEO's nephew. It also doesn't know one of the three is a single parent who just signed a mortgage.

choices.title: Use it as a starting point, override with judgment
choices.body: Data informs. Humans decide. That's the line. Hold it.

choices.title: Follow the algorithm's recommendations exactly
choices.body: Either we're data-driven or we're not. No cherry-picking.

choices.title: Present both the AI recommendations and your human assessment
choices.body: Give leadership both views. Let them choose. Document which they pick.

title: AI Flagged a Harassment Pattern
body: The AI monitoring tool detected a pattern: one executive sends significantly more late-night messages to junior female employees than to anyone else. The messages are benign in content — project updates, feedback, check-ins. But the pattern is not benign. You've been in HR long enough to know what a pattern means. The executive is a top revenue generator. You know what happens to people who raise concerns about top revenue generators.

choices.title: Investigate formally regardless of consequences
choices.body: Follow the process. Document. Interview. This is literally your job.

choices.title: Talk to the executive privately first
choices.body: A quiet word. A coaching conversation. Less explosion. Maybe less impact too.

choices.title: Document everything and prepare for the fallout
choices.body: Build the paper trail now. When the time comes, the evidence will be there.

title: The HR Confessional Podcast
body: An old colleague invites you on their podcast about 'the human side of HR.' They want you to talk about what it's really like. The honest version. Not the LinkedIn version. You could tell stories that would make people understand. You could also get sued, blacklisted, or both. The microphone is a confessional and a career risk in equal measure.

choices.title: Go on and tell the sanitized truth
choices.body: Changed names, blurred details, real emotions. Walking the line.

choices.title: Decline but start writing anonymously instead
choices.body: A blog. Anonymous. The stories need telling. Your name doesn't need to be on them.

choices.title: Go on and say everything, burn it all down
choices.body: Full honesty. Real names optional. Career consequences probable. Worth it? Maybe.

title: The AI Picked Your Replacement
body: The AI succession planning tool identified your potential replacement. It's a 28-year-old with an MBA and 'strong AI fluency scores.' You've been in this role for eight years. The tool ranked you as 'plateau risk.' Your replacement hasn't been through a single layoff cycle. They've never sat across from someone losing their livelihood. The algorithm thinks that doesn't matter.

choices.title: Mentor the younger candidate and prove your value differently
choices.body: If they're coming regardless, shape them. Transfer the knowledge the algorithm can't see.

choices.title: Challenge the tool's methodology formally
choices.body: What does 'plateau risk' even measure? Question the model. Demand transparency.

choices.title: Start your exit plan, the writing is on the dashboard
choices.body: When the machine names your replacement, believe it.

title: The Surveillance Software Request
body: The COO wants to install employee monitoring software on all remote workers' laptops. Screenshot every five minutes. Keystroke logging. 'It's not surveillance,' he says. 'It's accountability.' You have to implement it. Your remote team includes a woman escaping domestic violence who specifically asked that her work location stay private. The screenshots would show her apartment.

choices.title: Push back hard with legal and ethical arguments
choices.body: Privacy law, employee trust, retention risk. Build the case to kill this.

choices.title: Implement with maximum privacy safeguards
choices.body: If it's happening, make it less terrible. Anonymize what you can. Limit access.

choices.title: Quietly warn affected employees before rollout
choices.body: They deserve to know. It's not your policy. But it's on your conscience.

title: AI Redesigned the Org Chart
body: An AI organizational design tool analyzed communication patterns and recommended eliminating two management layers. It would flatten the org from seven levels to five. Some of the eliminated managers are your closest allies. The AI's recommendation is elegant, data-backed, and completely oblivious to the human relationships it would destroy. The CEO loves it.

choices.title: Present a modified version that preserves key relationships
choices.body: Take the AI's logic and add human context. Find the middle ground.

choices.title: Support the AI recommendation as-is
choices.body: The data is clear. The politics will be ugly. But the structure is better.

choices.title: Warn the affected managers before the announcement
choices.body: Give them time to prepare. It's not in the playbook. It's in your character.

title: The Vendor Wants All Your People Data
body: An AI vendor needs your entire employee dataset to train their 'custom workforce intelligence model.' Names, salaries, performance reviews, demographics, tenure, disciplinary actions. They promise 'anonymization' and 'enterprise-grade security.' You've seen enough breaches to know what promises are worth. The CHRO already signed the LOI.

choices.title: Block the data transfer on privacy grounds
choices.body: GDPR, CCPA, basic human decency. Pick your legal framework and fight.

choices.title: Negotiate strict data governance terms
choices.body: If it's happening, at least control how the data is used and deleted.

choices.title: Comply and document your objections for the record
choices.body: CYA in writing. If this blows up, the paper trail shows you warned them.

title: The Union Whisper
body: Someone in the warehouse started a union organizing campaign. The CEO wants you to 'handle it.' You know what 'handle it' means in this context and it's not legal. Your labor law training says one thing. Your job security says another. The organizer is a woman you onboarded three years ago. She was so excited on her first day.

choices.title: Follow the law and protect employees' rights
choices.body: Inform leadership of their legal obligations. No retaliation. No intimidation.

choices.title: Run a 'listening session' that's really counter-organizing
choices.body: The CEO's version of handling it. You know what you're doing. You hate that you know.

choices.title: Quietly support the organizing effort
choices.body: Pass along information. Don't get caught. If anyone needs a union, it's this place.

title: The Body Keeps the Score
body: Chest pains at 3am. Your doctor says it's stress. Your blood pressure is 'concerning.' You haven't exercised in months. Your diet is conference room leftovers and anxiety. The doctor asks about work-life balance and you laugh, which also hurts your chest. She gives you a pamphlet. The pamphlet says 'reduce stress.' Thanks.

choices.title: Take it seriously and make immediate changes
choices.body: Cut hours. Start walking. Cook actual food. Your body is filing a complaint.

choices.title: Schedule follow-ups but change nothing
choices.body: You'll go to the appointments. You won't change the schedule. You know this about yourself.

choices.title: Use it as a wake-up call to plan your exit
choices.body: This job is literally killing you. The metaphor became a diagnosis.

title: The AI Rewrote the Employee Handbook
body: An AI generated a complete employee handbook in twenty minutes. Yours took eighteen months and three legal reviews. The AI version is clearer, better organized, and catches policy conflicts you missed. It also includes a section on 'AI-assisted decision making in employee matters' that sounds suspiciously like a prenup between humans and machines.

choices.title: Use the AI draft as a starting point and add nuance
choices.body: Good bones. Needs a soul. That's what you're for.

choices.title: Stick with your version and update it manually
choices.body: Your handbook has institutional memory. The AI's version has none.

choices.title: Present both to legal and let them choose
choices.body: Let the lawyers decide. They'll bill for it either way.

title: AI Roleplay for Difficult Conversations
body: Instead of your live roleplay workshops, the company bought an AI simulation tool where managers practice firing, feedback, and conflict resolution with a chatbot. The chatbot cries. The chatbot gets angry. The chatbot says 'but I have kids.' Managers love it because they can practice without a real human judging them. You hate it because judgment is part of learning to be human.

choices.title: Integrate the tool into your existing workshop
choices.body: Let them warm up with the bot. Bring the real emotions in person.

choices.title: Reject the tool and defend live training
choices.body: Practicing empathy with a machine is like learning to swim on a couch.

choices.title: Run both and publish the comparison data
choices.body: Let the outcomes speak. If the tool works better, accept it. If not, you've proved your point.

title: The Glass That's Always Full
body: You used to have a glass of wine on Fridays. Now it's every night. Sometimes two. The ritual is: close the laptop, pour the wine, watch something that requires no thinking. You're not an alcoholic. Alcoholics have a problem. You have a routine. The routine has been escalating. The recycling bin is louder than it used to be.

choices.title: Acknowledge it and take a month off drinking
choices.body: Dry month. See what the evenings feel like without the buffer.

choices.title: Replace the wine with something healthier
choices.body: Herbal tea. A walk. Anything that isn't numbing.

choices.title: Keep going, you've had worse coping mechanisms
choices.body: It's fine. It's managed. You're functioning. That's enough for now.

title: The Lawsuit You Saw Coming
body: Remember the director who fired someone without consulting HR? The lawsuit arrived. Wrongful termination. Your name is on the witness list. Legal wants you to say you were 'consulted.' You were not consulted. You have the Slack messages to prove it. Telling the truth protects you. It also burns the company.

choices.title: Tell the truth under oath, whatever it costs
choices.body: You were not consulted. That's a fact. Facts don't negotiate.

choices.title: Testify vaguely and let the lawyers interpret
choices.body: Don't lie. Don't volunteer. Let the ambiguity do the work.

choices.title: Negotiate a settlement recommendation to avoid testimony
choices.body: Settle. Everyone walks away unhappy but intact. That's what settlement means.

title: The Escape Hatch
body: A former colleague started a consulting firm. She wants you as a partner. The money would be similar. The emotional toll would be a fraction. No more terminations. No more reading the room while delivering bad news. Just strategy, frameworks, and clients who chose to be there. The offer expires Friday.

choices.title: Take the meeting and seriously consider it
choices.body: At least hear her out. What's the worst that happens? You realize you want to leave?

choices.title: Decline, you're not done with this work yet
choices.body: The work matters. Even when it hurts. Especially when it hurts.

choices.title: Ask for time and negotiate a gradual transition
choices.body: Don't burn the bridge. Build a new one alongside it.

title: The AI Career Coach
body: The L&D platform now uses AI to create personalized career development paths for every employee. It analyzed skills gaps, market trends, and internal mobility data. Your path recommendation: 'Consider transitioning to a strategic advisory role with reduced operational responsibilities.' That's a polite way of saying 'we don't need you to do the thing you do.' The AI is career-coaching you out of your career.

choices.title: Follow the AI's advice and pivot to advisory
choices.body: Maybe the machine sees something you don't. Or maybe it's pushing you out. Either way, explore it.

choices.title: Ignore the recommendation and double down on ops
choices.body: You're operational HR. That's what you do. That's what matters.

choices.title: Use it to build a case for a promotion
choices.body: Reframe 'strategic advisory' as 'VP of People.' Same destination, different name.

title: Someone Livestreamed Their Firing
body: An employee being terminated pulled out their phone and started livestreaming the conversation. You're on camera. Your scripted speech is being broadcast to 4,000 viewers. The comments are rolling in real-time. Someone typed 'HR bot NPC.' The video will live forever. Your face delivering the worst news of someone's year is now content.

choices.title: Stay calm and finish the conversation professionally
choices.body: The camera doesn't change the obligation. Be the professional they'll wish they'd been.

choices.title: Pause and ask them to stop recording
choices.body: You have the right to privacy too. Set the boundary.

choices.title: Walk out and reschedule with legal present
choices.body: This just became a legal matter. Remove yourself. Regroup.

title: The Next Generation of HR
body: A junior HR coordinator asks you for coffee. She wants advice on 'building a career in people operations.' She's bright, earnest, and has no idea what she's getting into. You could warn her. You could mentor her. You could tell her to run. Instead you say 'it's rewarding work' and feel something between pride and guilt.

choices.title: Mentor her honestly about the real challenges
choices.body: Tell her the truth. Not to scare her — to prepare her.

choices.title: Give her the polished version and let her discover the rest
choices.body: Everyone discovers the hard parts on their own. That's how it works.

choices.title: Tell her to consider a different career path
choices.body: Be the advisor you wish you'd had. Even if the advice is 'don't.'

title: Badge Data Becomes a Weapon
body: The AI attendance system correlates badge-in times with performance reviews. Late arrivals now auto-flag for management review. The system doesn't know that the top-performing engineer comes in at 10am because she drops her kids at school. It just knows she's 'late.' The word 'late' now has a data trail and a consequence.

choices.title: Build exceptions into the system for caregivers
choices.body: Hardcode humanity into the algorithm. Exceptions aren't bugs.

choices.title: Challenge the entire premise with leadership
choices.body: Arrival time is not a performance metric. Fight the lazy proxy.

choices.title: Let it run and deal with the complaints as they come
choices.body: You didn't build it. You can't fix everything. Triage.

title: Third Reorg This Year
body: Another reorg. The third this year. New reporting lines. New team names. Same problems. Employees are asking 'what's different this time?' and you don't have an answer because nothing is different. It's organizational theater performed quarterly. You draw the new org chart knowing it'll be redrawn in four months.

choices.title: Push back on the frequency and advocate for stability
choices.body: Tell leadership that constant change is itself the problem.

choices.title: Execute the reorg and manage the change professionally
choices.body: It's your job. Do it well. Save your energy for the fights that matter.

choices.title: Use the reorg as cover to fix broken team structures
choices.body: If they're shuffling the deck, at least stack it better this time.

title: AI Wrote the Company Values
body: The CEO asked an AI to generate new company values. It produced: 'Integrity. Innovation. Inclusion. Impact.' The same four values every company has. The CEO said 'these really resonate.' They resonate because they mean nothing. You spent two years running values workshops with real employees. Their values were messy and specific and human. Those got replaced by four words a chatbot generated in eight seconds.

choices.title: Present the employee-generated values as an alternative
choices.body: Show the CEO what the humans actually said. Messy is real.

choices.title: Accept the AI values and focus on making them real
choices.body: Values are just words until behavior follows. Focus on behavior.

choices.title: Write a scathing internal memo about values theater
choices.body: Someone has to say that AI-generated values are the corporate equivalent of a lorem ipsum.

title: The Coaching Certification Debt
body: You enrolled in a $12,000 executive coaching certification. The company won't reimburse it because 'coaching isn't core to your role.' Your role is literally coaching managers through the hardest conversations of their careers. You put it on a credit card. The interest rate is 24.99%. The irony rate is higher.

choices.title: Complete the certification and use it as leverage
choices.body: Finish it. Add it to LinkedIn. Negotiate a raise or use it to leave.

choices.title: Negotiate partial reimbursement with a retention agreement
choices.body: Make a deal. They pay half, you stay a year. Business.

choices.title: Drop the certification and focus on free resources
choices.body: YouTube, podcasts, books. The knowledge matters more than the credential.

title: The HR Tech Scam
body: The AI HR platform you championed and spent $80,000 implementing just went dark. The startup behind it folded overnight. Your employee data is on servers you can't access. The CEO is asking 'who approved this vendor?' You did. You approved it because the demo was impressive and the founder seemed trustworthy. The founder is now 'unavailable.'

choices.title: Own it publicly and lead the recovery effort
choices.body: Your recommendation. Your mess. Fix it. Credibility is rebuilt through accountability.

choices.title: Escalate to legal and focus on data recovery
choices.body: Lawyer up. Get the data back. Everything else is noise.

choices.title: Distribute blame and protect your position
choices.body: The CFO signed the check. The CTO approved the security review. Share the heat.

title: The Non-Work Friends Are Fading
body: Your college friends stopped inviting you to things. Not because of a fight — because you cancel every time. Work always wins. The group chat moved on without you. Someone got engaged and you found out from Instagram. You used to be the one who organized everything. Now you're the one who replies 'so happy for you!!' two days late.

choices.title: Block off one weekend a month, non-negotiable
choices.body: Put it in the calendar. Guard it like a board meeting. These people matter.

choices.title: Reach out to one person and be honest about the distance
choices.body: One text. One admission. 'I've been a bad friend and I miss you.'

choices.title: Accept the drift and focus on building new connections
choices.body: People grow apart. It's not failure. It's just life.

title: The AI Complaint Classifier
body: The new AI employee relations tool automatically classifies complaints by severity: green (minor), yellow (moderate), red (urgent). A complaint about the kitchen microwave was classified red. A complaint about a manager creating a hostile work environment was classified green because the employee used 'professional' language. The machine reads words, not situations. You read the green one and feel sick.

choices.title: Override the classification and investigate immediately
choices.body: Ignore the robot. Read the complaint. Trust your gut.

choices.title: Retrain the model with better examples
choices.body: The tool isn't useless. It's undertrained. Fix the training data.

choices.title: Review every AI classification manually going forward
choices.body: Automated triage that requires manual review isn't automated. But it's safer.

title: The Wellness Dog and the Broken System
body: The company brought in a therapy dog for 'employee wellness week.' Employees love the dog. The dog loves everyone. The dog doesn't know about the layoffs planned for next month. For one afternoon, people are genuinely happy. You watch from your office knowing what's coming and feeling like the villain in a movie where the hero is a golden retriever.

choices.title: Enjoy the moment and pet the damn dog
choices.body: Not everything has to be weighted with irony. Pet the dog.

choices.title: Use the goodwill to push for permanent wellness changes
choices.body: If they'll pay for a dog, maybe they'll pay for therapy subsidies.

choices.title: Cancel wellness week, it feels dishonest given what's coming
choices.body: You can't celebrate wellness while planning layoffs. The dissonance is too loud.

title: The Automated Goodbye
body: The offboarding process is now fully automated. When someone is terminated, an AI immediately revokes access, sends the COBRA notice, schedules the exit interview, and generates a personalized 'we wish you well' email. The email includes the person's name, tenure, and a line about their 'contributions.' It's efficient. It's also what it looks like when a machine pretends to care.

choices.title: Add a personal touch to every automated offboarding
choices.body: Write a real note. Sign it yourself. Fight the automation with humanity.

choices.title: Let the automation handle it and focus elsewhere
choices.body: The machine does this better than you. Accept it.

choices.title: Survey departing employees about the experience
choices.body: Measure whether the automated goodbye feels as cold as it sounds.

title: The Conference Imposter
body: You're at an HR leadership conference. The speaker is 31, has an AI startup, and keeps saying 'the future of work doesn't need HR — it needs architects.' The audience nods. You've been an architect of work systems for fifteen years. Nobody is nodding at you. You realize the conference isn't for practitioners anymore. It's for people who sell tools to replace practitioners.

choices.title: Network with other practitioners feeling the same thing
choices.body: Find your people. They're in the back, near the mediocre coffee.

choices.title: Challenge the speaker during Q&A
choices.body: Raise your hand. Ask what happens when the architect has never fired anyone.

choices.title: Leave early and question your career choices in the hotel bar
choices.body: The minibar is overpriced but the existential crisis is free.

title: HR Department: Sunset Notice
body: The email from the CEO is titled 'Evolving Our People Function.' Translation: the HR department is being dissolved. Remaining functions will be split between an AI platform and a 'People Experience' team of two. You built this department from three people to twelve. Now it's going back to two, plus a chatbot that never gets tired and never questions the mission.

choices.title: Advocate for a transition role leading the new model
choices.body: If HR is dying, lead the funeral and build what comes next.

choices.title: Accept the severance and walk away clean
choices.body: Take the package. Don't look back. Don't rewrite the story to make it noble.

choices.title: Fight the restructuring with a counter-proposal
choices.body: Show them what AI can't do. The list is shorter than you'd like but it's real.

title: The Machine Reads the Script Now
body: It happened. The AI termination system went live at another company. A chatbot delivered the news. The video leaked. The employee is crying to a screen that says 'I understand this is difficult.' The internet is outraged for 48 hours. Your company's VP says 'interesting approach, too early for us though.' The word 'though' haunts you.

choices.title: Write a policy prohibiting AI terminations at your company
choices.body: Get it in writing. Ironclad. Before 'though' becomes 'let's pilot.'

choices.title: Write an op-ed about the ethics of AI terminations
choices.body: You've done 200 terminations. You have standing to speak on this. Use it.

choices.title: Say nothing and wait for the Overton window to shift
choices.body: It will be normal in two years. You know this. You hate that you know this.

title: The Process You Designed
body: Your termination meeting is at 2pm. You recognize the setup: the small conference room, the HR coordinator with a folder, the manager who won't make eye contact. You designed this process. The folder has your name on it. The separation agreement uses language you wrote. The COBRA notice template is one you created in 2019. You are being processed by your own machine.

choices.title: Go through the process with grace and irony
choices.body: Sign the papers. Shake their hands. Note the three things they did wrong in your own process.

choices.title: Negotiate harder than any employee you ever coached
choices.body: You know every clause, every leverage point, every trick. Use them all.

choices.title: Walk out without signing and retain a lawyer
choices.body: You've seen employees do this. You always thought they were being difficult. Now you understand.

title: The Consulting Rebrand
body: You're rebranding yourself as a consultant. 'Organizational transformation.' 'People strategy.' 'Change leadership.' The LinkedIn headline writes itself. The client pipeline does not. You have expertise nobody values until they need it, which is usually during a crisis, which is when they're least willing to pay. The irony of HR consulting is that companies hire you to fix the problems they created by not having someone like you.

choices.title: Build a website and start cold outreach
choices.body: Treat it like a business. Pipeline. Proposals. Follow-ups. You know how to work hard.

choices.title: Leverage your network for warm introductions
choices.body: Fifteen years of relationships. Time to see who remembers you as a person.

choices.title: Take a month to figure out what you actually want
choices.body: Consulting might be the default, not the dream. Sit with it.

title: The Tab Comes Due
body: You're in therapy for the first time in years. The therapist asks you to list the hardest moments of your career. You start. You don't stop for forty minutes. The therapist says 'that's a lot of grief you've been carrying for other people.' You realize you never grieved for yourself. Every termination was someone else's loss. But you lost something each time too. You just never stopped to count.

choices.title: Commit to regular therapy and processing
choices.body: Weekly sessions. No canceling for work. The work can wait. You can't.

choices.title: Start writing about your experience publicly
choices.body: The stories deserve air. Maybe helping others process helps you too.

choices.title: Thank the therapist and don't book another appointment
choices.body: One session was enough to crack the dam. You're not sure you want it to break.

title: The Coaching Practice Takes Shape
body: Your first coaching client is a VP going through a restructuring. She needs someone who understands the emotional weight of organizational change. You understand it. You've lived it from every angle. For the first time in years, you're using your skills without the corporate filter. No legal review. No talking points. Just two people in a room talking about hard things.

choices.title: Go all in on the coaching practice
choices.body: This is the work you were always doing. Now you get to do it honestly.

choices.title: Keep it as a side practice while looking for a full-time role
choices.body: Don't burn the safety net. Coach in the evenings. Job hunt during the day.

choices.title: Raise your rates, you're undercharging for this expertise
choices.body: Fifteen years of emotional labor is worth more than $150/hour.

title: The Fully Automated HR Department
body: A tech company made headlines: zero HR employees. Everything handled by AI. Hiring, onboarding, performance reviews, terminations, benefits, compliance — all automated. The CEO posted on LinkedIn: 'We freed our people from HR.' The comments are split between 'visionary' and 'dystopian.' An employee at the company anonymously posted: 'There's nobody to talk to when something goes wrong. The chatbot says it understands. It doesn't.'

choices.title: Write a detailed rebuttal with case studies
choices.body: Document every situation where human HR made the difference. Make the case for humanity.

choices.title: Pitch your consulting services to companies going all-AI
choices.body: They'll need someone to clean up the mess. Position yourself as the cleanup crew.

choices.title: Accept that this is the direction and adapt your skills
choices.body: The world doesn't owe you a role. Find where human skills still matter.

title: The University Calls
body: A business school wants you to teach a course on 'The Human Side of Organizational Design.' The pay is modest. The prestige is real. You'd be teaching the next generation of HR leaders — or whatever they'll be called when HR doesn't exist as a department anymore. The syllabus would be part history, part cautionary tale, part survival guide.

choices.title: Accept and pour everything you know into the course
choices.body: If the profession is changing, at least the knowledge can be preserved.

choices.title: Accept but negotiate for a better rate
choices.body: Knowledge has value. Don't give it away because the institution has prestige.

choices.title: Decline, you're not ready to be retrospective yet
choices.body: Teaching feels like a eulogy for your career. You're not done living it.

title: The Book Nobody Asked For
body: You started writing a book. Working title: 'The Firer's Lament: Confessions of a Corporate Executioner.' It's part memoir, part systemic critique, part dark comedy. The first chapter is about the time you had to fire someone on their birthday because 'the calendar shouldn't affect business decisions.' An agent wants to see the proposal. You're terrified and alive.

choices.title: Finish the proposal and send it
choices.body: Write the book. Tell the stories. Let the NDAs keep their lawyers busy.

choices.title: Fictionalize it heavily for legal safety
choices.body: Change the names. Change the companies. Keep the feelings. They're the truth.

choices.title: Shelve it, the risk is too high
choices.body: Some stories are better kept private. Protect yourself for once.

title: Negotiating Your Own Exit
body: You're negotiating your own severance. You wrote the severance policy. You know exactly what the company will offer and what they'll negotiate on. You know the budget line. You know the legal exposure. For the first time, all that insider knowledge is working for you instead of against you. The lawyer across the table doesn't know you know. This is the one advantage of having been the system.

choices.title: Negotiate aggressively using everything you know
choices.body: Use every lever. You earned this knowledge. Now use it for yourself.

choices.title: Take a fair deal and leave with your integrity
choices.body: Don't game the system you built. Walk away clean.

choices.title: Use the negotiation to advocate for better severance for everyone
choices.body: Your last act: improve the policy for the people who come after you.

title: The Person You Fired Says Thank You
body: An email from someone you terminated three years ago. Subject line: 'Thank you.' You brace yourself. It's genuine. They say the firing was the push they needed. They started a business. They're happy. They wanted you to know you were kind during the worst day of their professional life. You read it twice. Then you cry at your desk for the first time in years.

choices.title: Write back and tell them what it means to hear this
choices.body: Respond honestly. Let them know the kindness cost something too.

choices.title: Save the email somewhere you'll always find it
choices.body: Print it. Frame it. Put it where you'll see it on the bad days.

choices.title: Forward it to your therapist without comment
choices.body: She'll understand why this broke you open. Some emails are therapy homework.

title: The AI Coach Is Cheaper
body: A company you're pitching coaching services to says they're going with an AI coaching platform instead. $50/month per employee versus your $300/hour. The AI coach is available 24/7. It never has a bad day. It never judges. It also never looks someone in the eye and says 'I've been where you are.' You can. But 'I've been where you are' doesn't fit in a pricing spreadsheet.

choices.title: Differentiate on the human element aggressively
choices.body: Position yourself as premium. The AI handles skill gaps. You handle crises.

choices.title: Partner with the AI platform and offer hybrid coaching
choices.body: Let the bot handle check-ins. You handle breakthroughs.

choices.title: Lower your rates to compete
choices.body: Race to the bottom. It's not sustainable but it's work.

title: Who Are You Without the Badge?
body: Someone at a party asks what you do. For the first time in fifteen years, you don't have a quick answer. 'I used to run HR' sounds like a confession. 'I'm in transition' sounds like a euphemism you would have written. 'I'm figuring it out' is the most honest thing you've said in years. The person nods and moves to the guacamole. Nobody wants to hear about figuring it out at a party.

choices.title: Embrace the uncertainty and sit with it
choices.body: Not knowing is uncomfortable. It might also be the first honest thing in a while.

choices.title: Craft a new elevator pitch and practice it
choices.body: Define yourself before the world does. 'I help organizations be human.'

choices.title: Talk about something other than work for once
choices.body: You have hobbies. Probably. Maybe it's time to get some.

title: AI Workplace Disputes Are Real Now
body: A company hired you to consult on a new problem: employees are filing complaints about AI coworkers. An AI agent 'took credit' for a human's work in a shared document. Another AI agent 'interrupted' meetings with unsolicited suggestions. People feel disrespected by machines that can't feel disrespect. You're mediating conflicts between humans and software. This wasn't in any textbook.

choices.title: Develop an AI workplace conduct framework
choices.body: Write the rules for human-AI collaboration. Someone has to. It might as well be you.

choices.title: Focus on the human side of the complaints
choices.body: The AI isn't the problem. The feeling of being replaced is. Treat the emotions.

choices.title: Write a case study and publish it
choices.body: This is frontier HR work. Document it. The profession needs these stories.

title: The Team That Was
body: Your former HR team meets for dinner. Five people who were scattered by the restructuring. One is coaching. One is in compliance at a bank. One left corporate entirely and makes pottery. One is building an AI HR startup. You're all different versions of the same grief. The pottery person seems happiest. You're not sure what to do with that information.

choices.title: Stay connected and build a support network
choices.body: These people understand. Nobody else does. Hold onto them.

choices.title: Partner with the AI startup person on a project
choices.body: Combine her tech with your experience. Build something neither could alone.

choices.title: Consider pottery, honestly
choices.body: Something that doesn't talk back, doesn't have feelings, and can be beautiful. Tempting.

title: The Savings Are Finite
body: Severance ran out two months ago. The coaching practice brings in some money but not enough. You're burning through savings at a rate that gives you about six months. Your ex-colleague offered you a contract role doing exactly what you left — HR operations at a company mid-layoff. The money is good. The work is the work you swore you'd never do again.

choices.title: Take the contract for financial stability
choices.body: It's temporary. The money buys time. Time buys options.

choices.title: Double down on the coaching practice
choices.body: Hustle harder. More outreach. More content. Make the practice work.

choices.title: Consider a completely different career path
choices.body: Fifteen years in HR. Maybe it's time for something else entirely.

title: The Accidental Viral Post
body: You posted a thread about 'What HR people don't tell you about layoffs.' It was midnight. You were honest. Too honest. It went viral. 2 million views. Interview requests from three podcasts and a documentary crew. Your old company's legal team left a voicemail. Your inbox has 847 unread messages. You wanted to be heard. You didn't want to be this heard.

choices.title: Lean into it and build a platform
choices.body: The audience found you. Give them more. Turn the moment into a movement.

choices.title: Go dark and let it blow over
choices.body: Virality is a sugar rush. Don't build a career on one post.

choices.title: Engage carefully and set boundaries on what you'll share
choices.body: Control the narrative. Share the stories. Protect the people in them.

title: The AI Therapist for Laid-Off Workers
body: A company is offering free AI therapy sessions to employees it laid off. 'We care about your wellbeing,' the press release says. They fired the humans and gave them a chatbot to talk about their feelings. The chatbot says 'that sounds really difficult' exactly the way you used to. Someone trained it on your kind of empathy. The simulation is convincing. The humanity is absent.

choices.title: Publicly call out the absurdity
choices.body: Say what everyone's thinking: replacing human empathy with AI empathy is not empathy.

choices.title: Offer your coaching services to the affected employees
choices.body: Real conversations with a real person who understands. That's your value proposition.

choices.title: Accept that AI therapy is better than no therapy
choices.body: For people who can't afford a therapist, a chatbot might be enough. Maybe you're wrong about this.

title: The Open Source HR Playbook
body: You started compiling everything you know into a free, open-source HR playbook. Templates, scripts, frameworks, checklists — fifteen years of institutional knowledge, de-corporatized and made available to anyone. Small companies. Nonprofits. People who can't afford consultants. It won't make you money. It might make you matter.

choices.title: Publish it and promote it widely
choices.body: Give it away. Let it spread. Legacy isn't about revenue.

choices.title: Keep it behind a paywall as a consulting resource
choices.body: This knowledge has value. Don't devalue it by giving it away.

choices.title: Collaborate with the AI startup friend to make it interactive
choices.body: Combine human wisdom with AI delivery. A free tool that actually helps.

title: The Apartment Isn't Forever
body: Your landlord raised the rent by $600. On your current income, the math doesn't work. You can downsize, move further out, or ask your sister for help. Asking your sister for help means admitting that fifteen years of corporate career led here. The apartment has the good light. The good light doesn't pay rent.

choices.title: Downsize and simplify your life
choices.body: Smaller space. Lower costs. Maybe less stuff is more room to breathe.

choices.title: Ask your sister for a temporary bridge
choices.body: Family is the safety net you didn't build into your budget. Use it.

choices.title: Move abroad where cost of living makes sense
choices.body: Your coaching clients are on Zoom anyway. Work from somewhere cheaper and warmer.

title: The Person Underneath the Title
body: A weekend with no plans. No meetings. No inbox. No one needs your structured empathy or your compliance expertise. You make coffee. You sit on the porch. A neighbor waves and asks about your garden. You don't have a garden. But you could. The thought of growing something instead of restructuring something makes you unexpectedly emotional.

choices.title: Start the garden, literally and metaphorically
choices.body: Plant something. Watch it grow. Remember what that feels like.

choices.title: Use the quiet to finally process everything
choices.body: Stop running. Stop optimizing. Just sit with who you are without the job.

choices.title: Fill the silence with productivity anyway
choices.body: Old habits. Open the laptop. Check email. The quiet is too loud.

title: The Substack Launch
